top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B002) is the most bounded and mature achievement on the slate. The 1997 collateral-constraint paper has two authors, so credit leaves out no originator. It has nearly three decades of use in theory, quantitative macro and policy modelling. Its mechanism, in which collateral values feed back on credit and turn temporary shocks into persistent ones, is distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and runs. I treat adjacency to a prior prize as a balance question and not a merit demerit. The main weakness is that direct identification of the size of the amplification is weaker than the theory's influence, and I rest the case on originality, durability and breadth of use, not on settled magnitudes. I rank P002 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, B012) second. It is a mature, widely adopted measurement framework, but its credit is open to the Bresnahan, Benkard and Levin question, and a narrowly worded citation only partly answers that. I still rank it above no award because it is a substantive, well-tested contribution. P000 is last because the shortlist contains at least one achievement that meets the standards of maturity and attribution.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for Kiyotaki, Moore, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn; none is among my listed co-authors. I disclose only that I share Lund University with Tommy Andersson, an explicit supporter of P002, and that my economic-history work on electrification and railways is not adjacent to either proposal. Disclosed without adjudication.
